presenterNotes: Emphasize that writing linear equations from two points is a fundamental skill that appears in all modeling problems.
The comparison of two linear models (break‑even point) is a common real‑world application. Encourage students to graph both lines to visualize which is cheaper for different quantities.
Distinguish between line of fit (hand‑drawn estimate) and line of best fit (technology‑generated). The latter is more accurate.
Always remind students that correlation does not imply causation, and predictions are only valid within the range of the data.

explanation: A [[kw:linear function]] can model a situation where the rate of change is constant. Its graph is a straight line.
The [[imp:slope]] $m$ is the rate of change. The [[imp:y‑intercept]] $b$ is the starting value (when $x = 0$).
If you know the slope and y‑intercept, use $$y = mx + b$$
If you know the slope and one point $(x_1, y_1)$, use $$y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$$ (point‑slope form).
If you know two points, first find the slope with $$m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$$ then use point‑slope form.

blocks.title: Comparing Two Linear Models
teacherCues: Write two cost equations on the board: $y = 10x + 600$ and $y = 12x + 300$. Ask: Which one is cheaper per item? How can we find when they cost the same?
Demonstrate setting the expressions equal and solving for x.

explanation: Many real‑world problems involve comparing two linear models, like the total cost from two companies.
Each model is of the form $y = mx + b$, where $m$ is the [[imp:variable rate]] (cost per item) and $b$ is the [[imp:fixed cost]] (rental fee).
To find which is cheaper per item, compare the slopes. The smaller slope means a lower per‑item cost.
To find the [[kw:break‑even point]] (where costs are equal), set the two equations equal and solve for $x$: $$m_1 x + b_1 = m_2 x + b_2$$
For $x$ values below the break‑even point, one is cheaper; above it, the other is cheaper.

notes: Set the two cost expressions equal.
Check: plug $x$ back into either equation to find the equal cost.

explanation: A [[kw:line of fit]] is a straight line drawn on a scatter plot to model an approximately linear trend.

To create a line of fit by hand: 1) Make a scatter plot. 2) Sketch a line that passes through the 'middle' of the points—about as many above as below. 3) Pick two points on that line (they don't have to be data points). 4) Write the equation using the two points.
The line of fit is an estimate; different people may draw slightly different lines.
Use the equation to [[imp:predict]] $y$ for a given $x$, but only within (or close to) the range of the data.

notes: Use two points on the sketched line, not necessarily data points.
The slope and intercept are approximations.
Use the equation only within the data range to avoid extrapolation.

blocks.title: Line of Best Fit and Correlation Coefficient

explanation: The [[kw:line of best fit]] (or linear regression line) is the line that minimizes the sum of the squared vertical distances from the data points. It is more precise than a hand‑drawn line of fit.
The [[kw:correlation coefficient]] $r$ measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship. It ranges from $-1$ to $1$.
• $r$ close to $1$: strong positive correlation (points rise to the right).
• $r$ close to $-1$: strong negative correlation (points fall to the right).
• $r$ close to $0$: weak or no linear correlation.
You can use technology (graphing calculator or statistical software) to compute the line of best fit and $r$. The important skill is interpreting the output.

notes: The slope and intercept are computed to minimize squared errors.
$r$ close to $\pm1$ indicates a strong linear pattern.
$r$ close to $0$ indicates little to no linear pattern.
formulaCard.title: Interpretation of the Line of Best Fit

confusionCorner.body: Even if $r$ is near 1, the model only shows an [[imp:association]], not that time causes tuition to rise. Other factors (inflation, funding) are at play. [[imp:Don't claim causation from a linear model.]]

explanation: **Understand**: We have data pairs $(x, y)$ where $x$ is years after 2005 and $y$ is average tuition. A regression line has been computed: $y = 382x + 11,386$ with $r \approx 0.99$.
**Solve**: The slope $382$ means tuition increases about $382 per year. The $y$-intercept $11,386$ is the modeled tuition in 2005. For 2020 ($x=15$), $y = 382(15) + 11,386 = 17,116$.

**Conclude**: The model predicts average tuition of about $17,116 in 2020. Because $r$ is very strong, we can be confident in this prediction, but remember it's based on past trends and may not account for future changes.
